viewing_check: Armitage estimate A$30-50, current bid A$15 (seen 9 Nov ~6:02 pm). Only one book matters: open Traffics and Discoveries, check for Macmillan London 1904 on the title page with no reprint line on the verso and any ads at the back (dated 25.8.04 = first issue). Tauchnitz or Doubleday = A$10-20. Even a rebound first is A$30-80, so this is a decorative-shelf lot; sensible ceiling about A$70-90 all-in. Also read the leaning brown cloth book with the illegible spine and check the pocket volumes for an inscription (Gorringe's sold an inscribed Pocket Kipling for GBP120 in Jan 2024).

viewing_check: Armitage estimate A$60-90, current bid A$55 (seen 9 Nov ~6:04 pm). Priority 1: Biggles in the Baltic and Biggles Air Commodore. Baltic: one asterisk on the half title, 1940 on the title page, russet pictorial cloth with aircraft, red top edge = first (A$200-400 without jacket). Two asterisks or a thin volume = 1941-42 reprint (A$15-40). Air Commodore: blue-blocked sea-planes on the front and biplane on the spine, thick 5 cm spine, no 'reprinted' line = first (A$100-250). The plain tan cloth with script lettering in the photos points to reprints for both. Priority 2: the three jacketed late titles (Takes Charge 7/6 flap, Buries a Hatchet 8/6 flap and pale blue boards, Goes Alone with 'First printed 1962' only; its jacket spine number 61 matches the first) are worth A$45-80, A$40-80 and A$40-90 respectively if firsts. If all OUP books are reprints but the three jacketed books are firsts, the lot is worth about A$150-250; if Baltic is a one-asterisk first, A$350-600. Also lift Biggles Goes Alone to read the full title of the large Dean laminated book underneath ('The BIG...' label, rope-bridge cover): probably The Boy Biggles, but it could be another Dean title or an omnibus. If it is The Boy Biggles, laminated boards mean a 1970s reprint (A$5-15); the 1968 first is green cloth in an unpriced jacket with '(c) Capt. W. E. Johns 1968' and the Ludgate Hill imprint on the title page (A$40-80). Also glance at Biggles Flies to Work (Dean original first 1963 was blue boards in jacket; laminated = reprint, ignore) and the jacketed Special Air Police (green cloth Dean issue; Thames 1953 first is blue cloth, so the lot copy is a reprint, A$5-15). Bid ceiling suggestion: if no first confirmed, stop around A$90-110 plus premium; if the three jacketed late books are firsts, A$150-200; if Baltic or Air Commodore is a true first, up to A$300-400.

viewing_check: Nothing here needs collation: no firsts, limited editions or signatures expected. At viewing just check (1) slipcases for sunned spines, splits and stains, (2) cloth for fading and bumped corners, (3) that each book is in its own slipcase and nothing is a book-club or ex-library copy, and (4) for any numbered Folio Limited Edition or signed bookplate slipped in (none visible in the 5 photos). Current bid A$75 (9 Nov ~6:05 pm) is about A$92 with the 22% premium, or about A$8 a volume. Fair to about A$120-140 hammer if you want them on the shelf; above about A$150 you are paying retail for an auction lot.

unflagged_recheck: Re-checked all 12 titles: every one is a Folio Society reissue (Folio editions c.1994-2018) of a book first published elsewhere, in standard trade Folio binding. None is a Folio Limited Edition (those are numbered, quarter leather, larger format and would be described as such), none is signed, early Australiana or early children's, and none is a multi-volume set. The 'first' points are the original trade publishers (e.g. Ruskin's Stones of Venice, Smith Elder 1851-53, 3 vols; Jan Morris Venice, Faber 1960), not these. Folio '1st thus' printings carry no meaningful premium over later Folio printings (both sell about A$10-30 each). Nothing flagged.

MDCCCLXX(?) with final numerals partly handwritten, so 1878-1880; Armitage says 1878.", 'first_edition_points': "Not first editions and none are in play. Routledge's Birket Foster illustrated poets (Wordsworth, Milton, Scott, Longfellow, Goldsmith/Gray etc.) first came out 1853-1858 and were reprinted for decades. Imprint dating: 'George Routledge and Sons' (the '& Sons' style dates from 1865 on); 'The Broadway, Ludgate' was Routledge's London address from about 1866; '416 Broome Street' New York was used roughly 1866-1880s. So the photographed Wordsworth is a c.1866-1880 reprint, consistent with an 1878 prize. Value points instead are: full calf (not half calf) with gilt Harrow crossed-arrows arms on the front board, matching set binding, complete printed Harrow prize plate in every volume with the same recipient and date. description: BOX OF ENGLISH LITERATURE & LANGUAGE REFERENCE
titles: Richard Garnett & Edmund Gosse, English Literature: An Illustrated Record, Vol. I (From the Beginnings to the Age of Henry VIII), Heinemann, red cloth gilt, no jacket; Garnett & Gosse, English Literature: An Illustrated Record, Vol. II (From Henry VIII to Milton), Heinemann, red cloth gilt, no jacket; Edmund Gosse, English Literature: An Illustrated Record, Vol. III (From Milton to Johnson), Heinemann, red cloth gilt, no jacket (small chip at head of spine); Edmund Gosse, English Literature: An Illustrated Record, Vol. IV (From Johnson to Tennyson), Heinemann, red cloth gilt, no jacket; The Oxford Library of English Usage, 3 vols (I Grammar, II Spelling, III Usage), OUP c.1991, maroon cloth/boards in slipcase, no jackets; The Oxford Library of Words and Phrases, 3 vols (I Quotations, II Proverbs, III Word Origins), OUP c.1990s, maroon boards in slipcase, no jackets
flagged: {'title': 'Richard Garnett & Edmund Gosse, English Literature: An Illustrated Record, 4 vols (Heinemann, red cloth gilt)', 'why': "Only item in the box with an edition question. A 1903 Heinemann first-issue set is worth a little more than the 1906 Heinemann reissue or the later US printings (Grosset & Dunlap, seen dated 1904 and 1908, Macmillan 1923/1931/1935 with the Erskine supplement), but the gap is small (tens of dollars, not hundreds). Flagged so the dates get checked, not because it is a hidden prize. No auction record for a plain publisher's-cloth set was findable; dealer asks for complete red-cloth sets run GBP31-58 (1906) to US$137 (1903). Fine bindings (Bickers tree calf, Morrell half calf) ask GBP300+ but this copy is publisher's cloth.", 'first_edition_points': "Title page: 'English Literature / An Illustrated Record / in Four Volumes', each volume naming its period (Vol I 'From the Beginnings to the Age of Henry VIII' by Richard Garnett; Vol II 'From the Age of Henry VIII to the Age of Milton' by Garnett and Gosse; Vol III 'From Milton to Johnson' and Vol IV 'From the Age of Johnson to the Age of Tennyson' by Gosse). Imprint 'London: William Heinemann' (the US co-issue reads New York: The Macmillan Company), dated 1903 on the title page for the first issue; Vols II and IV were reviewed in the Spectator on 16 Jan 1904 at 16s per volume, so all four were out by end 1903 (some catalogues give 1903-04). Large 8vo/small 4to (c.255 x 180 mm), pagination Vol I xv+368, Vol II xiv+389, Vol III xii+381, Vol IV xiii+462. Colour frontispiece with tissue guard in each volume plus further colour and b/w plates, facsimiles and text illustrations. Publisher's red cloth, gilt-decorated spine and front board, top edge gilt, other edges untrimmed. No dust jacket expected (none recorded). Later states: Grosset & Dunlap NY printings, which can carry 1904 on the title page (eBay AU item 317555095881, sold 18/19 Oct 2026, shows a Grosset & Dunlap title page dated 1904), so a 1903 or 1904 date alone does not prove the Heinemann first; the imprint 'London: William Heinemann' is the deciding point; Heinemann 1906 reissue (PBFA set dated 1906 with Vol IV still dated 1903, so mixed dates occur); Grosset & Dunlap NY 1908 'fourth printing' red cloth (Chaparral Books listing); Macmillan NY 1923/1931 revised with John Erskine's supplementary chapter on 1892-1922 in Vol IV (brown cloth); Macmillan 1935 four vols in two.", 'value_if_first': "A$50-75 for a complete 1903 Heinemann red-cloth set in VG order, less for the Vol III spine chip. SOLD evidence is thin: one genuine 1903 Heinemann single, Vol I, sold on eBay AU for GBP8.79 (about A$17) on 24/25 Sep 2026, which implies roughly A$70 for four sold singly. Anything above A$75 rests on dealer ASKING prices only: Reader's Books, Petworth, 1903 first, red cloth gilt, VG, US$137.53 = A$209 (withdrawn); Once Upon A Time Books 1903-04 set US$80 = A$122 (sold out, undated). Retail asks typically run 2-3x auction results. No dated auction SOLD record for a cloth set could be found.", 'value_if_later': 'A$35-70 for a 1906 Heinemann reissue or a US printing (Grosset & Dunlap 1904/1908, Macmillan 1923/1931). SOLD: one Grosset & Dunlap 1904 single volume on eBay AU at GBP5.49 (about A$11) on 18/19 Oct 2026. ASKING: C L Hawley PBFA, Heinemann 1906 set GBP31.20 = A$62; Schooner Books, Heinemann 1906 set GBP57.85 = A$116; Chaparral Books, Grosset & Dunlap 1908 set US$65 = A$99; Second Story Books, Macmillan 1931 set US$93.75 = A$143.', 'check_at_viewing': "Open the title page of all four volumes and read the imprint first, then the date. 'London: William Heinemann' dated 1903 = first issue. Heinemann dated 1906, or mixed 1903/1906 = reissue. 'New York: Grosset & Dunlap' = later US printing even when dated 1903 or 1904 (a 1904 Grosset & Dunlap copy is recorded). Macmillan, or any Vol IV with John Erskine's supplementary chapter = later. Also check each colour frontispiece and tissue guard is present, plates not removed, hinges sound, the size of the Vol III spine chip, and foxing on prelims. School prize plates add nothing."}

The only book in the lot with any first-edition premium is a true 1978 first printing of book 1. So the 'One' copies are almost certainly the 1980 reissue, not the 1978 first.", 'first_edition_points': "Book 1 first published September 1978 in NZ (Evening Post / INL Print, Wellington), titled 'Footrot Flats' with no word-number on the cover. Look for the imprint page to read 1978 with no 'Reprinted' lines. Any copy titled 'One' (1980 reissue) or with 'Over x million in print' roundels is a later printing. title_notes: Footrot Flats albums were printed in huge numbers (the '4' covers themselves say over two/six million in print). Only Footrot Flats 1 in true 1978 first printing carries any premium, and dealer asking prices for it are only about US$17-66 (A$26-100), so below the A$100 flag threshold. Volumes 3-14 and Weekender: no first-edition premium, A$5-15 each. Note that 'Footrot Flats One' and 'Two' are the October 1980 retitled reissues (Wikipedia series list). The 1978 first of book 1 is titled plain 'Footrot Flats'. No early Australiana, signed, limited or fine-binding items were seen.

title_verdicts: Strong as Death: not valuable. 1920s/early-30s US reprint (series carries 1917 copyright) of a public-domain translation; A$5-15.; Mont-Oriol: not valuable, same series reprint.; Queen Hortense and Other Stories: not valuable, same series reprint.; Ball of Tallow and Other Stories: not valuable, same series reprint.; The Inheritance and Other Stories: not valuable, same series reprint.; Unread 6th Maupassant volume (back left, photo 1): same series by its label, not valuable.; Six framed prints (canal/townscape, 'Le ...' woodcut-style print, waterfall, coastal/sunset, birches with bluebells, small stockyard/cattle scene with hand-inked caption): decorative, not book items; stockyard scene worth a glance in case it is an original watercolour, but tiny and low value either way.
boxes_note: Described as 2 boxes but only a single tabletop spread is photographed (5 photos). Only 6 books are visible and all are one Maupassant set; any further books in the boxes were not photographed. Rest of the visible contents is bric-a-brac: lustre ceramic trout figure with a small clock/thermometer, paua/abalone shell desk clock, black Art Deco style vase with blue flower, glass rolling pin, gilt compact, brass items, buttons, Osmiroid Basic Calligraphy Set, napkin ring, Bryant & May matchbox, ribbon box, shaving brush, crochet piece, egg cup.
value_no_firsts: A$40-80 resale for the whole lot. The 6 Maupassant volumes are worth maybe A$30-60 as a decorative shelf group (perhaps a bit more if all 10 of the series are present). The paua shell desk clock and lustre trout clock might bring A$20-40 each locally, the prints a few dollars each.
viewing_check: Estimate $30-50, current bid $15. Nothing here meets the 'first edition worth hundreds' rule on the photos. At viewing, only worth a look if the second box holds unphotographed books: rummage it for anything pre-1900, Australiana, signed or children's. For the Maupassant set just count volumes (10 in the full set) and check condition; the title pages will say French Library Syndicate with 1917 copyright, which is a later reprint, not a first. Glance at the small stockyard picture to see whether it is original watercolour or a print.

spine_check: confirmed, nothing missed. Second reader re-opened all 5 photos full size (1637156_1 to _5) and zoomed every book. Green cloth with ornate gilt series spine, no jacket", 'why': 'Was flagged only because the decorative binding looked older than the rest of the box. It is one volume of the University of Knowledge (Wonder Books) multi-volume educational set, edited/published in Chicago in 1938-40. These sets were sold widely by subscription and survive in large numbers; single volumes are common, low-value second-hand stock. Not a candidate under the A$100 test.', 'first_edition_points': "Book-specific checks (from general knowledge of the series, not verified against a bibliography this run): (1) Title page: 'Art in the Middle Ages' by Joseph Pijoan, imprint University of Knowledge Incorporated, Chicago, with the 1940 date. (2) Verso: copyright 1940 with no later copyright, reprint or 'printing' line. A later date or a statement of a later printing means a reprint, but even the first printing is low value. (3) Plates: the series volumes are illustrated with photogravure (sepia/monochrome) plates and some colour plates. Flick through and check none are torn out or cut; any list of illustrations should match. Missing plates reduce it to near nil. (4) Set status: almost certainly a lone volume of the set (no other matching green gilt Wonder Books spines visible in the photos). Single volumes sell cheaply; only a complete or near-complete set in bright gilt is of any interest, and even then it is a modest decorative lot rather than a collector's book. There is no 'first edition' premium for this title.", 'value_if_first': "About A$10-30 for a single 1940 first-printing volume in good cloth with plates complete (general knowledge, NOT confirmed by comps this run; the lot file's own figure is A$10-20). Then put it back and move on. It cannot change the A$30-50 lot estimate. Spend the viewing time on the real unknown in this lot, the maroon gilt cloth book standing upright between the two boxes (lot 228 t2), plus the Dali by Dali endpapers and the flat items at the bottom of each box.', 'source': 'lot_228_t1.json'}; {'title': 'Unidentified maroon cloth book with gilt spine lettering, standing upright between the two boxes (title not readable; not identified)', 'why': "The only older-looking plain cloth book in two boxes of mostly modern art reference and literary titles. It might be early Australiana, a limited or private-press edition, or an older art monograph. The chance is low. Most maroon gilt-lettered cloth books in an art-reference box turn out to be 1920s-1960s publisher's cloth (Batsford, Studio, Medici Society, Phaidon, Faber, Angus & Robertson) that has lost its jacket, worth A$10-40 (the same range used in value_if_later).", 'first_edition_points': "No title, so there are no title-specific points. General checks for a maroon gilt-lettered cloth book: (1) Title page: title, author, publisher, city and date. A dated title page before about 1920, or an Australian imprint before about 1940 (Sydney/Melbourne: Angus & Robertson, George Robertson, Lothian, Art in Australia Ltd, Ure Smith, Fanfrolico Press, Hawthorn Press), is the interesting case. (2) Limitation: a limitation statement ('This edition is limited to ... copies, of which this is No. ...'), usually on the half-title verso, title verso or the final leaf (colophon), with a number written in, and possibly a signature. Australian art books of the 1920s-40s from Art in Australia, Ure Smith (e.g. the Lionel Lindsay, Norman Lindsay, Hans Heysen, Streeton, Elioth Gruner volumes) and the Fanfrolico Press often came in limited numbered issues and are the realistic way this book reaches hundreds. (3) Verso: 'First published' with no later dates is good; 'Reprinted', 'Second edition', 'New impression' or a list of years means a later printing. An ISBN or a date after about 1970 means it is ordinary stock. (4) Binding: original publisher's cloth, gilt bright, no library labels, stamps or rebinding. A plain maroon library binding (buckram, often with a library number on the spine) is worth little. (5) Contents: tipped-in colour plates, original etchings or woodcuts, or a loose signed print; check plates against the list of illustrations, since missing plates kill the value. (6) If the spine or title says 'Vol. II' of a set, it is close to worthless on its own.", 'value_if_first': 'Not priceable without the title, and NOT backed by any comp (no SOLD, ASKING or ESTIMATE found or checked this run; see searches_tried). Treat these as guesses to test at the viewing, not as prices. No jacket visible in the photos, so price as no-jacket.', 'value_if_later': 'A$10-40 (later printing, library binding, odd volume or common 20th-century art monograph without jacket; unverified estimate, no comps). This is the most likely outcome.', 'check_at_viewing': "Pull the maroon book standing upright between the two boxes and read the spine and title page. Only chase it if it says 'limited to ... copies' with a number written in, is signed, has original prints (etchings, woodcuts, tipped-in signed print), or is Australian and pre-1940 (Art in Australia, Ure Smith, Fanfrolico, Angus & Robertson, George Robertson etc.); otherwise ignore it. Either way, photograph the spine, title page, title verso and any limitation/colophon leaf so the eBay sold and AbeBooks checks can be re-run on the actual title before the lot closes (Wed 11 Nov 2026, 1:15 pm AEDT). flagged: {'title': 'A.G. Steel & R.H. Lyttelton, Cricket (The Badminton Library), Longmans, Green 1888 and later editions', 'why': "Common Badminton Library title with three quite different values. Ashford Press 1987 facsimile (the earlier box-photo read suggested this): about A$20-30. Longmans trade copies in brown pictorial cloth, first 1888 or later: tens of dollars at auction, A$50-180 asking. Only the 1888 large-paper issue (250 copies, mostly numbered) or a fine leather binding gets into the hundreds, and even the large paper has made only GBP50 hammer at Mullock's. The dated auction record is thin and low: single trade copies make well under A$100. Unless this is the large paper, it fails Andy's hundreds-or-thousands test.", 'first_edition_points': "First edition: title page 'Cricket' by A.G. Steel and the Hon. R.H. Lyttelton, with contributions by A. Lang, W.G. Grace, R.A.H. Mitchell and F. Gale, London: Longmans, Green, and Co., 1888, with NO edition statement. Trade issue is 8vo, about 19.5 cm tall, xiii, 429 pp, frontispiece plus 10 full-page plates (illustrations after Lucien Davis and photographs), publisher's adverts at the rear, brown pictorial cloth gilt, Longmans at the spine foot. Watch for later editions that look the same: a 'Second Edition' 1888 (confirmed by Knights 2021 and Antiquarian Auctions lots, so an 1888 date alone is not enough), 'Third Edition' 1889, 'Fourth Edition' 1890, 'Fifth Edition, thoroughly revised' 1893 (420 pp), 'Sixth Edition' 1898, and a 1904 issue. Large-paper issue: 1888, limited to 250 copies, normally numbered on a limitation leaf (one unnumbered copy is offered), clearly bigger (about 9.5 in / 24 cm, Christie's called it 4to), thick paper with uncut fore and bottom edges, top edge gilt, plates on India paper, xiv, 463 pp. It was issued in half (three-quarter) navy or blue morocco with gilt-decorated cloth boards and the Beaufort arms in gilt on the front board. Ashford Press Publishing, Southampton, 1987 facsimile: green cloth with gilt lettering, plates reproduced, the title page still reads Longmans 1888, so check the verso for an ISBN or Ashford Press imprint and look for a modern spine.", 'value_if_first': "1888 trade first in original brown cloth: A$50-120 at auction (no dated single-copy first trade hammer found; later trade editions sell at roughly NZ$75 / A$70 for two volumes), dealer asking about US$117 (A$180) for a very good copy. 1888 large-paper numbered copy in its original half morocco: A$100-400 at auction (Mullock's GBP50 hammer, about A$100, for a rebacked copy), dealer asking US$275-950 (A$420-1,440). Ashford Press 1987 facsimile: A$20-30.', 'check_at_viewing': "Measure it and open the title page. If it is about 24 cm tall on thick paper, with a limitation leaf numbering it one of 250 and the Beaufort arms on the front, it is the large paper and worth bidding to about A$200. If it is a normal 19.5 cm brown-cloth copy dated 1888 with no 'Second Edition' on the title page, it is the trade first, worth about A$80 at most. Any edition statement, or green cloth with an ISBN or Ashford Press on the verso, means it is worth about A$20-40, so leave it.", 'source': 'lot_237_t2_fill.json'}; {'title': 'Unidentified cricket hardback, brown cloth, no jacket (spine unreadable in photo 3) - base case A$20-60', 'why': "The only book in the box that looks older than about 1960, but nothing about it can be read from the photos: no title, author, publisher, year or size. Plain brown cloth with no jacket fits hundreds of pre-1960 books, so the honest base case is an ordinary 1930s-50s tour book, annual or cricketer memoir that has lost its jacket, worth about A$20-60. That does not meet Andy's hundreds-or-thousands rule. The only way it does is if it turns out to be an original Wisden Cricketers' Almanack hardback from a scarce year (above all the wartime 1939-45 years) or carries a genuine important signature. Nothing visible supports that, so treat Wisden as a long shot to rule in or out at the viewing, not as the expected outcome.", 'first_edition_points': "STEP 1, rule Wisden in or out in five seconds. An original Wisden hardback is small and very thick: roughly 17-18 cm tall, about 11-12 cm wide and 4-6 cm thick (1,000+ thin pages), brown/buff cloth, with 'WISDEN' and the year in gilt on the spine and the front board lettered or blocked. If the book is a normal-shaped octavo (around 20-22 cm tall, 2-3 cm thick) it is not a Wisden, skip to step 2. If it is Wisden: the title page reads 'John Wisden's Cricketers' Almanack for [year]' with an edition number (e.g. 'Seventy-Eighth Edition' = 1941) and the editor's name; the almanack for year X covers season X-1. Then check whether it is an original hardback, a facsimile or a rebound softback. Facsimile tells: a limitation or 'reprinted' statement on the verso or a front/rear leaf naming Willows Publishing (1990s onwards) or John Wisden & Co's own later reprints, bright white paper and crisp boards. Rebound softback tells: cloth and lettering that do not match the publisher's standard gilt spine, or the original paper wrappers bound in at front/back. Record the year: original hardbacks from 1939-1945 (especially 1941) are the only realistic route to four figures. STEP 2, any other title. Turn to the back of the title page (verso). A first printing shows only one date ('First published 19xx'); any 'Second impression', 'Reprinted' or later edition line means a later printing. A 1930s-50s cricket book without its jacket is a reading copy whatever the printing. STEP 3, always. Check the front free endpaper, half-title and title page for signatures or inscriptions, and any tipped-in team sheet; a genuine Bradman or full touring-team signature matters far more than the edition, but needs authentication before paying for it.", 'value_if_first': 'A$20-60 base case: unidentified 1930s-50s cricket hardback, no jacket, first or not (estimate, no verified comps; see searches_tried). Upside only if it is an original-cloth Wisden from a scarce year or bears a genuine important signature; no sourced prices for those were obtainable this run, so check them after the viewing once the year/title is known.', 'value_if_later': 'A$10-40 (later impression or reprint of an ordinary cricket book, no jacket; also covers a Wisden facsimile until a sold check is done for the specific year). title_verdicts: Royal Academy Pictures 1899/1900 and other years: not valuable. Common Cassell annual supplements, typically A$15-40 each; a run of 5-6 maybe A$60-120 retail.; Hutchinson's Britain Beautiful: not valuable. Common part-work bound volumes, A$10-25 each.; Churchill, History of the English-Speaking Peoples (Cassell): borderline. A complete 4-vol set of UK first impressions in jackets is asked at about GBP 61-76 (A$120-150) on AbeBooks; odd volumes or later impressions are A$10-20 each. Only reaches A$100+ if all four vols are present and are first impressions.; The Wonder Book of Empire: not valuable. Many editions, A$15-40.; Hawthorn, Challenge Me the Race: not valuable unless signed. Unsigned 1958 Kimber copies in jacket asked GBP 10-29 (A$20-60) on biblio; signed Hawthorn material (died Jan 1959) is the real money.; Hawthorn, Champion Year: not valuable unless signed or with tipped-in signature. First edition unsigned asked GBP 25 (A$50) at Simon Lewis.; Tour de France 1978 / Tour 80 / other Tour annual: not valuable. A$10-25 each to cycling buyers.; Ultimate Bicycle Book: not valuable. Common DK title, A$5-15.; Unidentified red bull-artwork book and middle-row cycling items: unknown, check on the day; nothing visible suggests value.
boxes_note: 1 box (contents partly spread on the floor in photo 1). 6 photos, all opened full size; photos 2-6 are close-ups of items also in photo 1. value_no_firsts: A$100-200 retail if sold piecemeal (Churchill set A$60-120 even as mixed impressions, Royal Academy Pictures run A$60-120, Hawthorn pair A$40-80, Tour annuals A$10-20 each), realistically A$80-150 for a quick sale. Comfortably above the $20-30 estimate.
viewing_check: Estimate $20-30, current bid $10. At viewing: (1) Open both Hawthorn books and look for any signature, inscription, or loose signed item; check the Challenge Me the Race verso for 1958 with no later impression. (2) Count the Churchill volumes, confirm all four, check each verso for 'First published' with no impression line. (3) Note the years of all Royal Academy Pictures volumes. (4) Read the middle-row cycling items and the red bull-cover book. Without a signature this is a A$80-150 lot; worth bidding to about A$60-80 all in.

title_verdicts: After Dinner Stories (Robey/Bateman): low. Common 1920s humour; worn, no jacket. Typical A$20-60 asking. Not A$100+; Poetical Works of A.L. Gordon: not valuable. Many reprints from 1912 on; only 1860s-70s first issues of his separate works matter (Sea Spray and Smoke Drift, Bush Ballads), not this collected edition; Cornwall (Claude Berry, County Books): not valuable, A$10-25; Oasis of the North (Macleod): not valuable, A$10-25; Beautiful Scotland (Haslehust, Blackie Beautiful series): low, A$15-40; slightly more in jacket. Not A$100+; Easy Steps / Men of Might: not valuable, Victorian/Edwardian school readers or a binder's volume, A$10-30; Tahiti: Island of Love (Langdon): not valuable, A$15-40 even as 1959 first in jacket; Gregory's Melbourne 1982-83: not valuable, nostalgia A$10-30; Lord Fisher book: unidentified; most Fisher titles (Memories 1919, Records 1919, Hough's First Sea Lord 1969, Bacon's Life 1929) are A$20-80. Check it is not signed or inscribed; Unidentified spines (5): unknown, check at viewing
boxes_note: 1 box, 2 photos: photo 1 is the whole box from above (about 11 spines + one book lying flat), photo 2 is a close-up of a Lord Fisher portrait plate lying on top of the books. Images 3+ return 404, so nothing else photographed.
value_no_firsts: A$30-80 for the whole box. About 8 identified low-value 1920s-1980s hardbacks plus 5 unidentified spines. Realistic resale is A$5-15 a book, and only the Robey/Bateman, Haslehust and Langdon would sell individually. Fine at the estimate, but there is nothing here to chase as a first edition.
viewing_check: Estimate $15-30, current bid $5 (+22% BP). At the viewing: (1) Read the 5 blank or worn spines: plain blue, pink, dark navy with red ribbon, the black item behind Tahiti and the black item lying flat at the front. (2) Identify the Lord Fisher book and look for any signature or inscription. (3) Robey: check for 1920 Grant Richards on the title page and any inscription. (4) Check whether Beautiful Scotland has its jacket. If nothing turns up, bid no more than about A$30-40 all-in.
searches_tried: None completed. The shared web search budget for this run was already used up (limit reached), so the verdicts come from general bookselling knowledge, not checked sold prices. No SOLD prices are quoted. No currency conversion was needed.
spine_check: confirmed, nothing missed. Second reader opened both photos (800x600, the largest the site serves; _3 and large/ paths 404) and zoomed every spine. All 9 readable spines match the first reader. The plain blue, pink/peach and navy spines show no lettering (navy has only two faded gilt bands near the head). The black textured strip at the front of the box shows no lettering; the red ribbon hangs from under the Gregory's/navy end. The black area with red and white print behind the Tahiti spine (also seen upside down in photo 2, bottom left) is probably the front or back panel of the Tahiti dust jacket rather than a separate book, so the unidentified count may really be 4. The Lord Fisher portrait in photo 2 looks like a loose sheet or plate (grey stock, white margin, caption at right) lying on top of the books, not necessarily a bound book; check at viewing whether it belongs to a book in the box.
flagged: {'title': 'Lot 306: (a) George Robey, After-Dinner Stories, with ten illustrations by H.M. Bateman (Grant Richards, London, 1920); (b) Admiral of the Fleet Lord Fisher, Memories and/or Records (Hodder and Stoughton, London, 1919), described as signed', 'why': 'Both titles are common and cheap unsigned. An unsigned Memories and Records pair sold for US$10 at a US auction in 2022. The only thing that could make this lot worth real money is a genuine ink signature or inscription by Fisher (he died 10 July 1920, so any real one dates from Oct 1919 to Jul 1920). Fisher autograph material does sell: a 4pp letter he signed in 1918 made GBP 550 at Bloomsbury in 2006. I found no sold record for a signed copy of Memories or Records, so the signed value below is a judgement anchored on that letter, not a direct comp. Both books reproduce Fisher letters and signatures in facsimile, so a printed signature is the main trap.', 'first_edition_points': "ROBEY: the first edition has Grant Richards Ltd, London, 1920 on the title page. The title reads 'After-Dinner Stories by Robey, with ten illustrations by H.M. Bateman'. 232pp, about 190 x 130 mm, brown cloth (Barter Books copy). Later issues: a Grant Richards 'reprinted' copy dated 1922 (World of Rare Books, red and brown cloth), and a Richards Press reissue of 1927 in yellow cloth with black lettering. Any Richards Press imprint, or a reprint line or 1922 date, means a later issue. Count the ten Bateman plates. MEMORIES: the title page reads 'Memories by Admiral of the Fleet Lord Fisher / Hodder and Stoughton / London New York Toronto / MCMXIX' (from the Gutenberg transcription). The frontispiece is captioned 'Lord Fisher, 1917, Admiral of the Fleet', from a portrait by J.C. Beresford. About 250 x 170 mm, xvi + 295pp, with photographic plates. Cloth colour varies between dealer descriptions (red cloth on the Barter copy, gilt-blocked cloth on others). RECORDS: Hodder and Stoughton, London 1919, black boards with gilt titles on the front and spine (David Ford copy). I did not find a reliable dealer description of later-impression wording. A 'second impression' or similar on the title or verso means a later printing. The US edition (Doran, New York, 1920, 2 vols as Memories and Records) is a separate, lesser edition. SIGNATURE: the preface ends with a printed 'FISHER.' and both books reproduce facsimile letters, so check that any signature is in real ink on a blank leaf (front endpaper, half-title or title) with pen indentation and ink sitting on the paper surface. Make sure an ink 'Fisher' is not just an owner's name; 'previous owner's inscription' is common in these copies.", 'value_if_first': 'Robey 1920 first, no jacket, worn: about A$20-50 at auction. Fisher with a GENUINE ink signature or inscription: roughly A$300-800 by judgement. A strong association inscription (to a naval or political figure) could do better. The 2006 GBP 550 (A$1,100) Fisher letter is a richer item than a signed book.', 'value_if_later': "Robey 1922 reprint or 1927 Richards Press reissue: A$10-30 (asking US$31-40 retail). Check the title page says Hodder and Stoughton MCMXIX with no 'impression' wording. For the Robey, the title page should say Grant Richards Ltd 1920, not 1922 or Richards Press, and all ten Bateman plates should be present. If there is no genuine Fisher signature, it is a A$20-60 lot and only worth a low bid.", 'source': 'lot_306_fill.json'}

viewing_check: Estimate A$20-40, current bid A$15. Not a books lot, so skip it unless you want the marbles or dolls. If passing: (1) Pigs Is Pigs, open the title page. You want 'McClure, Phillips & Co.' with MCMVI and 'Published, May, 1906' on the copyright page. Doubleday or no date means a reprint, so walk away. (2) Kookaburra-cover book, read its title, publisher and date; only worth noting if it is pre-1950 Australian. (3) Look under the Footrot Flats stack for any real comics (Australian 1950s Phantom or Frew, Marvel/DC); none are visible in the photos despite the description. (4) Tip out the marbles jar for handmade swirls or onionskins (pontil marks). (5) Check the dolls' necks and backs for maker marks.

flagged: {'title': 'Ellis Parker Butler, Pigs Is Pigs (New York: McClure, Phillips & Co., 1906) and later printings', 'why': "Pass unless it goes for close to nothing. Pigs Is Pigs sold in huge numbers and McClure ran at least six impressions within a year, so 1906 copies turn up everywhere. Plain 1906 McClure copies at US general auctions have hammered at US$10 to US$20 (LiveAuctioneers 2014 to 2024, including one sold with a jacket). Dealers ask US$25 to US$85 for McClure copies they call firsts, and one Fine Doheny-provenance copy is listed at US$150. The only money in this title is the 1905 to 1906 Railway Appliances Co. wrappered pamphlet printed before the McClure edition: US$160 for a rough copy in 2021, US$800 for two inscribed copies with provenance in 2024, and US$1,250 asked for a near fine copy. The old note's 'Published, May, 1906' point was wrong. The first McClure printing reads 'Published April, 1906'.", 'first_edition_points': "McClure first printing: the title page reads New York, McClure, Phillips & Co., 1906, and the verso reads 'Published April, 1906' with NO impression statement below it (Morgan Library and Texas A&M catalogue records). Later McClure printings add 'Second Impression', 'Third Impression' and so on, and the sixth impression is dated 1907. Any copy dated 1907 or 1908, or carrying a Doubleday, A.L. Burt or other imprint, is a reprint. Collation: [6], 37, [3] pages plus 5 plates by Will Crawford (frontispiece, then plates facing pp. 18, 20, 30, 34), 18 cm, publisher's tan or brown pictorial cloth with a black and white front design. Count the plates, because a missing plate kills it. True pre-first: a square, roughly 18 x 18 cm (7 in) pamphlet in stiff pictorial wrappers printed red and black, imprint Railway Appliances Company, Chicago (Dec 1905 first, Jan 1906 second), 20 unpaginated pages. Butler himself called these 'prior to First Edition' printings. A dust jacket on the McClure edition did not move the price at a 2023 sale (US$20).", 'value_if_first': 'McClure April 1906 first printing (no impression line), no jacket, VG: A$25-60 at auction (comparable hammers US$10-20, and none of those lots stated the impression). Dealer retail is A$40-130 asking, up to about A$230 for a Fine copy with provenance. Railway Appliances Co. wrappered pamphlet: A$250-500 for a worn copy at auction (US$160 hammer in 2021), and more if bright (A$1,900 asked for near fine).', 'value_if_later': 'A$10-40 (McClure second to sixth impression, 1906 to 1907, or a Burt or Doubleday reprint. Hammers of US$10-20, and dealers ask US$15-30 for 2nd and 3rd impressions).', 'check_at_viewing': "Turn to the back of the title page. 'Published April, 1906' with nothing under it is the first printing, but even then I would pay no more than about A$40. Any 'Impression' line, a 1907 date or another publisher makes it a A$10-30 reprint. Check all 5 Crawford plates are present. If it turns out to be the square paper-covered Railway Appliances Company pamphlet, that is a different book and worth A$250 or more.", 'source': 'lot_311_t1_fill.json'}

title_verdicts: Britannia Saxonica map: possibly worth A$100+. If it is a genuine 18th century copper engraving (for example one of the Rapin/Tindal History of England maps, or a Camden or Wells plate) it would sell for roughly A$80-250 retail depending on maker and condition. A modern reproduction would be worth about A$5. Not confirmed online because the search budget ran out; Bromeliad chromolithograph: moderate. Loose 19th century Belgian or French horticultural chromolithographs (Illustration Horticole, Belgique Horticole, Flore des Serres type) usually sell for A$30-120. The damaged mount reduces this; Chromolithograph that looks like a Tasmanian native laurel: possibly worth A$100+. If the bottom margin carries a Louisa Anne Meredith 'Bush Friends in Tasmania' imprint (Vincent Brooks Day & Son, or Hanhart) it is collectable Tasmaniana at about A$150-500 per loose plate. If it is a European or German chromolithograph it is worth about A$20-60. Identification and value are unverified; Eucalyptus coccifera print: low to moderate. If it is a Margaret Stones Endemic Flora of Tasmania plate, loose plates usually sell for about A$20-80 each. Several plates together would be a useful parcel; Second botanical print (yellow blossom): low to moderate, same reasoning as the Eucalyptus coccifera print; N.J. Caire Fitzroy Gardens greeting card: possibly worth A$100. Caire is a well-collected Victorian landscape photographer, and a gilt greeting-mount view in fair condition might fetch A$50-150. Unverified; Konrad (Launceston) cabinet card: not valuable. Launceston studio portraits fetch about A$10-30. Local interest only; Newman 'Atlantic' cabinet card: not valuable (about A$5-15, water stained); Other cabinet cards and CDVs: not valuable (about A$5-20 each unless the sitters are identified); School or children's group photo: not valuable, unless the school is identified as Tasmanian, which might give A$20-60; Settlement or sawmill township panorama: moderate. An identified Tasmanian or Australian mining or timber township could be worth A$50-200 to local history collectors. Unidentified it is worth about A$20-40. Check the back for a caption; Watermill photo with the 'Cork' label: probably Irish (Cork), worth about A$10-40. If the mill turns out to be Tasmanian it is worth more; Wedding portrait and the boy photo: not valuable; '...ERBY.' captioned item: possibly worth something. value_no_firsts: A$40-80. About 60 books: 18 Baldacci paperbacks are near worthless in bulk (A$1-2 each in a box lot); the useful part is ~10-15 Australian natural history and local history hardbacks in jackets (Haines, Lewis Salisbury, Warburton x2, Paull, Grant & Serle, Pizzey, Calder, Coleman) worth A$10-40 each retail but slow sellers, plus three fly-fishing titles A$10-30 each. viewing_check: Estimate $20-30, current bid $10, 22% premium, closes 2:51 pm Wed 11 Nov. Nothing in the photos meets the A$100+ first-edition test.
